title: Business Continuity Management (BCM)
description: How BCM keeps critical business functions running in a disaster: its goals, the business impact assessment, BCP and DRP plans, testing and restoration order.

nodes.title: Focuses on critical and essential functions of business
nodes.description:
BCM does not try to cover every business process and system, only the most critical ones.
In a disaster you usually cannot keep the whole business running as usual. So decide which processes and systems are most critical, and focus your limited resources on them.
BCM is the business process that drives planning and preparation for disasters:
1. Run the BIA (Business Impact Analysis).
2. Use its results, the measurements of time (RPO, RTO, WRT and MTD), to create BCPs (Business Continuity Plans) and DRPs (Disaster Recovery Plans).
3. Test the plans, train people on them, and maintain them.
The point is to keep critical processes and systems running during a disaster, so that the business survives.

children.title: Goals of BCM
children.description: The three major goals of BCM. Remember them in this order.

children.title: 1. Safety of people
children.description:
The number one, most important goal.
People are the most valuable asset of an organization. Without people there is no organization.

children.title: 2. Minimize damage
children.description: Minimize the impact and the damage the disaster causes.

children.title: 3. Survival of business
children.description: Help make sure the business survives.

children.title: Business Impact Assessment
children.description:
The BIA: the first major process in BCM. The page calls it both Business Impact Assessment and Business Impact Analysis.
It identifies the critical processes and systems, and produces the measurements of time that drive the BCP and DRP.
It also decides the restoration order.

children.title: Identify Critical Processes & Systems
children.description: The BIA identifies the most critical business processes and systems by consulting stakeholders from across the organization.

children.title: Measurements of Time
children.description:
The major output of the BIA: four measurements of time, approved by the process or system owner.
Each one is a measurement of time: seconds, minutes, hours, days.
On a timeline:
- RPO: the period before the disaster, from business as usual up to the disaster.
- RTO: from the disaster to recovery.
- WRT: from recovery back to business as usual.
- MTD: covers RTO plus WRT.

children.title: RPO
children.description:
Recovery Point Objective: how much data the organization is willing to lose in a disaster.
The maximum tolerable data loss, measured as time. If the server explodes, how much data can you lose? Examples: 5 seconds, 10 minutes, 3 hours or 2 days worth of data.

children.title: RTO
children.description:
Recovery Time Objective: the maximum tolerable time to recover systems to a defined service level.
Usually, how long it takes to bring the backup systems online.

children.title: WRT
children.description: Work Recovery Time: the maximum tolerable time to verify system and/or data integrity, as part of returning systems to normal operations.

children.title: MTD
children.description:
Maximum Tolerable Downtime, also called MAD (Maximum Allowable Downtime).
The maximum time a critical process or system can be disrupted before the consequences for the business become unacceptable.
The MTD is always greater than or equal to RTO + WRT.

children.title: Owner approval of #s and associated costs
children.description:
The owner of the process or system must approve the RPO, RTO, WRT and MTD numbers.
The reason: the owner pays for the recovery strategies needed to achieve those numbers.

children.title: Types of Plans
children.description: The two major types of plans. The measurements of time drive how they are written.

children.title: Business Continuity Plan (BCP)
children.description:
Focuses on critical business processes, and on the survival of the business.
Example: paying employees is usually a critical business process. If the automated payroll system blows up, the BCP covers how to keep paying employees.

children.title: Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP)
children.description:
Focuses on recovering critical technology, infrastructure and systems.
Example: if the payroll system explodes, the BCP keeps the payroll process running, while the DRP recovers the actual payroll system.

children.title: Testing Plans
children.description:
BCPs and DRPs must be tested periodically. A plan that was never tested and refined is unlikely to work in a real disaster.
Tests are usually done in order: start with the simplest test, refine the plan based on the results, then move up to the next, more complete test, and so on.

children.title: Read-through / Checklist
children.description:
The first and simplest test.
The author of the plan reads through it to make sure nothing is missing, going through a checklist. Example: are the call tree names and alternate contact details correctly written in the plan?

children.title: Walkthrough
children.description:
An entirely paper-based exercise.
Stakeholders from across the business sit around a conference table with copies of the plan and walk through it: page 1 says we do X, Y and Z.
The stakeholders are experts in their own areas (finance, customer relations, IT, business owners, etc.) and give feedback on the plan.

children.title: Simulation
children.description:
Also entirely paper-based, with stakeholders around a table with copies of the plan.
The difference: you invent a scenario, such as a virus outbreak or an earthquake at a location, and everyone must follow the plan as if the disaster were happening.
You add updates or twists from time to time (this data center just went offline, CNN is on line 3) to see how well the plan works.

children.title: Parallel
children.description:
The first test that actually touches systems: only backup systems, NOT production systems.
Scenario-based: people react to an invented scenario using the plan, for example by bringing backup systems online.

children.title: Full-interruption / Full-scale
children.description:
The final and most important test: you actually cause a disaster.
Example: to find out if the backup power system works when the power is cut, cut the power.
Only do it after every other test has passed, and with management's approval.

children.title: Restoration order
children.description: How to decide the order in which business processes and systems are restored.

children.title: Most critical first
children.description:
Restore the most critical processes and systems first.
Another important outcome of the BIA: business and system owners meet, argue it out, and decide which processes and systems are truly the most critical and in what order to restore them.

children.title: Dependency charts
children.description:
A system usually cannot be brought up on its own. You must consider what it depends on, and bring those dependencies up in the right order.
Dependency charts map this out.
